title: Heroic medicine

confidence.note: Rush's own 1794 account records his doses and bleedings, and the 1793 epidemic is well documented. That his treatment did more harm than good is the judgment of colleagues then and historians since, but he kept no records that could settle it.

summary: In Philadelphia's 1793 yellow fever epidemic, Benjamin Rush drained his patients of blood and purged them with mercury, and called it a cure.
body: Between August and November 1793 yellow fever killed 4,000 to 5,000 people in Philadelphia, about a tenth of the city. Benjamin Rush stayed while other physicians fled, and answered with 'depletion': purges of calomel, a mercury compound, and repeated bleeding. 'I drew from many persons seventy and eighty ounces in five days,' he wrote. He believed fever came from overexcited blood vessels, so emptying the body made sense to him. Critics charged that he killed more than he saved; he kept no records to test it. George Washington's fatal illness in 1799 got the same 'heroic' bloodletting and blistering.

links.note: Hahnemann's gentle doses were partly a reaction against depletion.
Pierre Louis later counted the results of bloodletting.
Yellow fever was later shown to be spread by mosquitoes.

title: Pinel, Pussin and the chains

confidence.note: Pinel's appointments to Bicêtre (1793) and the Salpêtrière (1795) and his 1801 treatise are documented. The famous scene of Pinel striking off the chains is contested: his own book credits the keeper Pussin, and we could not open a source fixing exactly who removed the chains, or when.

place: Bicêtre and the Salpêtrière, Paris, France
people: Philippe Pinel (1745–1826), physician at Bicêtre and the Salpêtrière
Pussin, lay governor (keeper) of the insane at Bicêtre
summary: Paintings show Philippe Pinel striking the chains off the mad. His own book gives much of the credit to the hospital's keeper, Pussin.
body: Philippe Pinel was appointed physician at the Bicêtre hospice in Paris on 25 August 1793, during the Revolution, and on 13 May 1795 moved to the Salpêtrière, with its 600-bed ward for the mentally ill. From these wards came his 'moral treatment' of insanity: close observation, conversation, routine and firm kindness instead of blows. In his treatise on mental alienation (1801; English translation 1806) he reported that at Bicêtre keepers were forbidden 'on any pretext whatever, to strike a madman', though strait-waistcoats and seclusion remained.

The legend that grew up around him, in paintings and popular prints, has Pinel personally freeing the chained insane. His book tells a more shared story. Pinel praised 'the zeal, the humanity, and intelligence of the keeper', the governor Pussin, and described Pussin, not himself, taming patients, once with servants rattling chains for effect. In England the Quaker-run York Retreat was pursuing similar moral treatment.

myth.tradition: In 1793 Philippe Pinel dramatically struck the chains from the insane at Bicêtre, single-handedly inventing humane psychiatry.
myth.record: Pinel's own treatise credits the lay keeper Pussin for Bicêtre's humane regime and still used strait-waistcoats; the solitary heroic scene was fixed by later paintings and prints.

links.note: Moral treatment inspired the 19th-century asylum building boom.
Pinel also taught at the new Paris school of health.
Rush in Philadelphia was treating madness with bleeding and purges.

title: Jenner and vaccination

confidence.note: Jenner's own 1798 Inquiry dates the Phipps vaccination to 14 May 1796. What remains uncertain is which virus he actually used: the modern vaccine is vaccinia, not cowpox, and old vaccine samples point to horsepox.

people: James Phipps, the eight-year-old boy first vaccinated
Sarah Nelmes, dairymaid whose cowpox sore supplied the matter
Benjamin Jesty, farmer who used cowpox on his family in 1774
summary: A Gloucestershire doctor tested a farmyard belief on an eight-year-old boy and gave the world vaccination, though nobody knows which virus was in his lancet.
body: Before 1796 the best protection against smallpox was variolation: deliberately infecting a healthy person with matter from a smallpox sore. It usually caused a milder illness than catching the disease, but it could kill, could set off new outbreaks, and needed a steady supply of smallpox patients. Country people had noticed something else. Dairy workers who caught cowpox, a mild disease that left pustules on the hands, seemed to escape smallpox. Reports of this circulated in the 1760s, and in 1774, during an outbreak at Yetminster, a farmer named Benjamin Jesty deliberately gave cowpox to his wife and two sons.

Edward Jenner, a country doctor in Gloucestershire, put the belief to a public test. On 14 May 1796 he took matter from a cowpox sore on the hand of a dairymaid, Sarah Nelmes, and inserted it through two shallow cuts into the arm of James Phipps, aged eight. The boy was briefly unwell. About six weeks later Jenner inoculated him with smallpox matter, and no disease followed. The Royal Society rejected his paper in 1797, so in 1798 he published *An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae* at his own expense, describing Phipps and 22 other cases.

The method, later called vaccination after the Latin *vacca*, cow, spread fast. By 1800 it had reached other European countries and the United States, passed at first from arm to arm; after 1860 vaccine was mostly grown on calves. Bavaria required it of army recruits in 1807. Britain outlawed variolation in 1840 and in 1853 made vaccination compulsory for children, provoking the first anti-vaccination movement. In 1980 the World Health Assembly declared the world free of smallpox.

Jenner was not the first to use cowpox, and he did not know what he was injecting. His contribution was the first systematic account of challenge experiments, published for others to check. He suspected the disease came from horses, and a 1902 American vaccine has turned out to be closely related to horsepox; the vaccinia virus of 20th-century vaccines is distinct from cowpox. Which virus Jenner used is unknown.

myth.tradition: Jenner discovered that cowpox protects against smallpox, and the vaccine he gave the world was cowpox.
myth.record: Farmers already knew of the protection and Benjamin Jesty used it in 1774; Jenner's achievement was testing and publishing it. The modern vaccine virus, vaccinia, is genetically distinct from cowpox, and Jenner's original virus is unknown.

links.note: Vaccination replaced the riskier practice of variolation.
Spain carried Jenner's vaccine across its empire in children's arms.
Vaccination eventually ended smallpox.
Pasteur extended the word and the idea to laboratory vaccines.

title: Hahnemann invents homeopathy

confidence.note: Hahnemann's 1796 paper and the 1810 Organon are dated publications. Modern reviews agree there is no reliable evidence that homeopathy works for any condition.

people: Samuel Hahnemann (1755–1843), German physician and chemist
summary: A German doctor disgusted with the dangerous drugs of his day proposed that like cures like, and that diluting a medicine makes it stronger.
body: Samuel Hahnemann quit practice for a time, finding the drugs of his day uncertain and often dangerous. In 1796 he published the paper that founded homeopathy, expanded in his *Organon* of 1810. Its rules: like cures like, so a substance that causes symptoms in the healthy can treat them in the sick; and the more a medicine is diluted, the stronger it becomes. Many remedies are diluted until no molecule of the original remains. Set beside bleeding and mercury purges, Hahnemann's regime of tiny doses, good food, exercise and fresh air looked gentle. Modern reviews find no reliable evidence that it works for any condition.

links.note: Homeopathy grew up as a gentle alternative to depletion.
Hahnemann's self-experiments with cinchona bark inspired 'like cures like'.

title: The birth of the clinic in Paris

confidence.note: The founding decree (4 December 1794), Bichat's books and Louis's 1835 study are all dated. Calling this the 'birth of the clinic' is a historians' framing of a gradual change, and the effect of Louis's numbers on practice is hard to measure.

people: Xavier Bichat (1771–1802), anatomist at the Hôtel-Dieu
Pierre-Charles-Alexandre Louis (1787–1872), physician at La Charité
summary: After the Revolution, Paris doctors followed patients from bedside to autopsy table and began to count their results.
body: The Revolution dissolved France's old medical faculties, and on 4 December 1794 the Convention founded new schools of health. Paris, with its huge hospitals, became the place to learn medicine: doctors examined patients on the wards, then followed them to the dissecting room. Xavier Bichat, who worked at the Hôtel-Dieu and died in 1802 aged 31, broke the organs down into their common materials, which he called tissues, and argued that each tissue could fall ill on its own. 'Open a few corpses,' he wrote in 1801, and the confusion of symptoms would clear.

The Paris doctors also counted. In 1835 Pierre Louis compared 77 pneumonia patients by when they had first been bled: about 44 per cent of those bled in the first four days died, against 25 per cent of those bled later. He concluded that bleeding had 'narrow limits' of usefulness. In 1833 alone, France imported 42 million medicinal leeches.

myth.tradition: Louis's statistics proved bloodletting useless and swiftly ended it.
myth.record: Louis concluded that bleeding helped in limited, severe cases; Broussais's leech doctrine was already in decline, and how much his numbers changed practice is unclear.

links.note: Morgagni had already tied symptoms to lesions found after death.
Laennec's stethoscope was a product of the Paris wards.
Louis's comparison of groups foreshadowed the controlled trial.

title: The Balmis expedition

confidence.note: The expedition's dates and route are well established in Spanish records; figures for the number vaccinated are rough, and little is known of the children's later lives.

place: From La Coruña, Spain, to the Americas, the Philippines and China
people: Francisco Javier de Balmis, Spanish military physician
Isabel Zendal, carer of the orphans
José Salvany y Lleopart, Balmis's deputy
summary: To carry Jenner's vaccine across an ocean, Spain shipped 22 orphans and passed the infection from arm to arm, one child after another.
body: In 1803 King Charles IV sent the military physician Francisco Javier de Balmis to carry Jenner's new vaccine to Spain's colonies. The vaccine could not be kept alive for the long voyage, so it travelled in people: 22 orphaned children sailed from La Coruña on the corvette *María Pita* and were vaccinated in turn, arm to arm. Their carer, Isabel Zendal, brought her own son. The expedition reached the Caribbean in February 1804 and split in Venezuela; José Salvany spent years vaccinating in South America and died there, while Balmis went on to Mexico, the Philippines and China, returning to Spain in 1806. None of the children came home.

links.note: The expedition carried Jenner's cowpox vaccine.
Smallpox had devastated the Americas since the conquest.

title: Sertürner isolates morphine

confidence.note: Sertürner's reports of 1805–06 and his 1817 paper are dated publications; the experimental work behind them stretched over years and cannot be pinned to a single date.

summary: A self-taught apothecary's assistant pulled the 'sleep-inducing factor' out of opium, isolating the first alkaloid and testing it on himself.
body: Medicines around 1800 were mostly crude plant preparations whose active ingredients came in unknown and varying amounts. Opium, used since ancient times, remained among the most important. Friedrich Sertürner, a young apothecary's assistant with little formal training, used ammonia to separate an almost pure 'sleep-inducing factor' from it. His first reports, in 1805 and 1806, attracted no attention. In 1817 he republished the work at length, calling the substance *morphium* after the god of sleep and dreams, and this time chemists took notice.

Sertürner had tested it on himself and three young volunteers: a quarter of a grain produced a happy light-headedness, while larger doses brought drowsiness and then confusion. He showed the substance was an alkali, overturning the belief that the active principles of plants were acids. Morphine was the first alkaloid isolated from any plant, the start of alkaloid chemistry, and it gave doctors a drug whose dose could be measured.

links.note: The syringe was soon used to inject morphine.
Morphine's descendants fuelled later addiction epidemics.
Purified plant drugs paved the way for manufactured ones.
